warmup.q: The payments database now runs on three machines. One takes every new payment, and the other two copy each one. So that no payment a card reader was told about can ever be lost, the first machine waits until both copies have a payment before it answers OK. Then one copy's machine freezes for 40 seconds, while the company that rents it out moves it to other hardware. What happens to card payments during those 40 seconds?
options: The first machine stops waiting for the frozen copy and waits only for the other one
Every payment waits until the frozen copy answers again, so payments stop for up to 40 seconds
Each payment fails at once with an error, so the card reader can try again
The other machines notice the frozen copy and remove it after a few seconds
warmup.why: The rule says "wait for both", so no payment can get its OK until both copies have confirmed it, and a frozen machine confirms nothing. Every card reader waits, and the slowest copy sets the speed for everyone. That's why real databases wait for one copy, or for a majority, and why some quietly stop waiting when a copy goes silent: MySQL, a popular database, does that after a timeout, as the second section shows. Skipping or removing a frozen copy is something a separate tool can add. The rule as written only waits.

sections.h: Why keep copies, and why one machine must decide the order
sections.html:
Let's see what one machine costs us. A computer that runs a program other programs reach over the network is a server. Ours runs PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies use, and three things go wrong.

First, its disk can die, or its building can lose power, and nothing records a payment until someone builds a new machine. Second, distance. The server is in Virginia, and a shop in Singapore opens its page of today's sales. Every question that page asks travels to Virginia and back, a round trip of more than 200 ms (thousandths of a second). Third, crowding. Month-end reports read millions of payments, competing with card payments for the same processor and disk.

All three have one answer: keep copies of the data on more machines. A copy in another building survives the dead disk. A copy near Singapore answers the shop's questions there. Five copies can answer five times as many questions. A copy that holds all of the data and keeps up with every change is a replica, and keeping replicas is called replication. (The Partitioning track splits the data into pieces; here, every replica holds all of it.) Copying data that never changes is easy: copy it once. The hard part is every change after that.

So let's try the simplest plan: the program that sends a change, the client, sends it to every copy itself. Two clients change payment pay-77 at almost the same moment. Client A says it was captured: the money really moved to the shop. Client B says it was refunded: the money went back to the customer. A sends at 0 ms and B at 1 ms. Copy X is 2 ms from A and 9 ms from B, so it hears captured, then refunded. Copy Y is 8 ms from A and 3 ms from B, so it hears them the other way round.

Each copy did exactly what it was told. Now copy X says the money went back, and copy Y says it didn't. Nothing will repair this later, because neither copy knows it's wrong.

The copies disagree because nobody decided the order. Picture a club's notebook of payments, with photocopies kept in two other towns. If each town took changes by phone from anyone, the copies would drift apart. So only one clerk writes in the notebook, and she numbers each line: 1, 2, 3. The towns copy her lines in number order, and never write their own.

Databases do the same. One machine, the leader, takes every change. It applies the change and adds it to the end of its log, a list of changes in the order they happened. Each entry gets the next number, its position in the log. The other machines are followers. Each reads the leader's log and applies the entries in strict position order. Two copies that start from the same data and apply the same entries in the same order end up with the same data. Changes go only to the leader; questions, called reads, can go to any copy.

The clerk is the leader, her numbered lines are the log, and each town's photocopy is a follower. The picture breaks in one place: everyone knows a town's copy is days behind, while nobody can see how far a follower is behind without asking.

That's single-leader replication. Keep its picture, one numbered log with each follower at some position in it, because the whole lesson builds on it. When may the leader say OK? How does a new follower start? What does a crash lose? Each is a question about positions.

Most databases work this way under their own names. PostgreSQL calls the leader the primary and a follower a standby, and its log is the write-ahead log (WAL). Go deeper lists the names in four other databases.

The leader decides the order. Next, we'll ask what decides the cost of a crash: the moment it says OK.

try.title: Two clients and no leader, then one leader
steps: From the labs folder, run the first command below. It plays the pay-77 story on pretend time inside one program, so it gives the same result on every computer. First each client sends its change to both copies. Then copy X becomes the leader, and copy Y follows its log.

The second command puts client B 3 ms from copy X and 9 ms from copy Y. Before you run it, predict: do the two copies agree without a leader this time? And if they do, is the plan without a leader safe?

try.expect:
Without a leader, the copies end up disagreeing. With one, they agree:

No leader: each client writes to both copies
    2 ms  copy X applies captured  (from client A)
    4 ms  copy Y applies refunded  (from client B)
    8 ms  copy Y applies captured  (from client A)
   10 ms  copy X applies refunded  (from client B)
  copy X says pay-77 is refunded, copy Y says captured
One leader (copy X): it puts the updates in its log, the follower (copy Y) applies the log in order
    2 ms  leader X logs position 1: captured  (from client A)
    8 ms  follower Y applies position 1: captured
   10 ms  leader X logs position 2: refunded  (from client B)
   16 ms  follower Y applies position 2: refunded
  leader X says pay-77 is refunded, follower Y says refunded

With -Pargs='3 9', both copies happen to hear the changes in the same order, so they agree. That's luck: the next pair of changes can arrive the other way round. With a leader, the order is written in the log, and every follower reads the same order.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: High availability, load balancing and replication

aside.title: So is a follower a backup?
aside.html: No, and the difference shows on a bad day. A follower copies every change, the wrong ones too. Delete every payment on the leader by mistake, and a few milliseconds later every follower has deleted them as well. A backup is a copy of the data from an earlier moment, kept apart, that you can go back to. The two help each other: a backup can start a new follower, as the third section shows, and lesson 4 builds both on PostgreSQL.

sections.h: When the leader says OK: before or after a follower has the payment
sections.html:
A card reader sends a payment to the leader, which writes it to the log on its own disk and sends the entry to the followers. At some moment, it tells the card reader OK. That's called acknowledging the write, and the moment a change becomes final is its commit. Which moment you pick decides what a dying leader can take with it.

The fastest choice is asynchronous replication: say OK as soon as the entry is on the leader's disk, and send it to the followers in the background. A follower is usually a few milliseconds behind, but nothing limits it. Busy with one huge change, catching up after a restart or stuck behind a slow link, it can be minutes behind. If the leader dies then, the payments in between exist on no running machine, although each card reader heard OK.

The safest-looking choice is fully synchronous replication: say OK only when every follower has confirmed the entry. Then any follower can take over and lose nothing. It breaks at once. Each payment waits for the slowest follower, and a frozen, restarting or cut-off follower stops every payment until it returns. That was the warm-up: one frozen machine stops payments for 40 seconds.

Most systems choose the middle: wait for some followers, not all. Wait for any one follower, and every acknowledged payment is on at least two machines. This is usually called semi-synchronous replication. Wait for a majority instead, two of three or three of five, and you have a quorum, which the Consistency and consensus track turns into a method called Raft.

The lab's simulator puts exact numbers on this. Follower f1 is 20 ms from the leader and f2 is 50 ms (one way, so a round trip to f1 takes 40 ms). A payment arrives every 4 ms, and the leader dies at 1,001 ms:

The leader says OK when Each payment waits OKs in the first second Lost when the leader dies
its own disk has it 0 ms 250 4
one follower has it 40 ms 241 0
both followers have it 100 ms 226 0

The waiting choices sent fewer OKs because their last payments were still waiting when the leader died. A cloud company rents out computers in regions, areas such as northern Virginia. Real round trips are about 1 ms between two buildings of one region and about 70 ms between regions, and the table keeps its shape.

"A follower has it" can mean three points, the last three boxes in the figure. The entry can have reached the follower's operating system, the program that runs all the others and writes files to disk when it chooses. It can be flushed, forced onto the follower's disk. Or it can be applied, so questions asked on the follower see it. PostgreSQL lets each change choose with its setting synchronous_commit: remote_write, on and remote_apply wait for those three points, and local only for the leader's disk (lesson 4 runs them). A follower of MySQL, another popular free database, confirms once the entry is flushed to its disk, before applying it.

Now the small print: what happens when no follower answers? A MySQL leader waits up to rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout, 10 seconds by default. Then, in the manual's words, it "reverts to asynchronous replication", and waits again only when a follower catches up. No card reader sees an error. One payment takes 10 seconds, every later one is fast, and the database is now asynchronous. The only sign is a status number, Rpl_semi_sync_source_status, dropping from 1 to 0.

PostgreSQL does the opposite: it keeps every payment waiting until a follower is back. Neither is wrong. MySQL keeps payments flowing and quietly drops its promise; PostgreSQL keeps its promise and stops the payments. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, has the same choice under its acks setting.

A setting's name describes a good day. Find out what it does on a bad one.

All of this assumes the followers already exist. Next, we'll build a new one while payments keep arriving.

Waiting for both now costs 140 ms: every payment pays for the farthest follower.

sections.h: A new follower starts from a snapshot and a position
sections.html:
Followers die and get replaced, and you add more as the number of questions grows. A new follower needs the leader's data, and the leader can't stop taking payments meanwhile. Copy the leader's files while payments keep arriving, and some parts of the copy are from 10:00 and others from 10:20: a mix the database was never in. Lock the leader so that nothing changes while you copy 2 TB, and payments stop for hours.

The way out is to remember exactly where the copy was taken. A snapshot is a copy of all the data as it was at one moment. Here's the recipe:

  1. Take a snapshot of the leader's data without stopping payments, and note the log position it matches.
  2. Copy the snapshot to the new machine and load it.
  3. Ask the leader for every entry after that position, and apply them in order.
  4. Once caught up, keep receiving new entries like any other follower.

The position is what makes the recipe work. Start one entry too late, and the follower lacks a payment forever, with nothing to tell it so. Start too early, and it applies entries it already has. If an entry says "add 30 cents to the fee", the fee is charged twice. (Lesson 2 shows which kinds of log survive that.)

Each database ships the recipe. PostgreSQL's command pg_basebackup copies the files while keeping every log entry written meanwhile. Replaying those brings the mixed-up files to one moment, and the follower carries on from there (lesson 4 builds one). MySQL has a clone plugin. MongoDB, a database that stores records as documents, runs an initial sync. A new follower of Redis, a database that keeps its data in memory, gets a snapshot file plus the writes made meanwhile.

The same position lets a follower that was away for a while catch up cheaply. It reconnects and says "send me everything after 4,812". The leader can do that only if it still has those entries, and that's a real trade-off.

Keep the log until every follower has it, and one follower that's down for a week fills the leader's disk. PostgreSQL's replication slots work this way. A slot is the leader's note of how far one follower has got, and the leader keeps every entry after it. That's why PostgreSQL 18 added a setting, idle_replication_slot_timeout, to give up on a follower that stays away too long (lesson 4).

Keep only a fixed amount instead, and a follower that falls further behind must start again from a new snapshot. MongoDB and Redis work this way. A Redis follower reconnects with PSYNC <replication id> <offset>, which names the history it was following and how far it got. If the leader still has everything after that offset, the follower gets only the missing part. Otherwise it gets a whole new copy.

Rebuilding a big follower is slower than the arithmetic says. GitHub is the website where many programmers keep their code. In its 2018 outage (next section), loading several terabytes from backup took hours, and the catch-up kept slowing down, so every estimate of recovery was wrong. Plan for hours, and keep a spare follower so you rarely rebuild in a hurry.

A spare follower is also what you need on the worst day, when the leader itself dies. Next, we'll crash it.

Before you read the output: when the link comes back, what tells f1 that it missed something, and what does it ask the leader for?

100 ms  leader at  11, f1 at  10

  300 ms  leader at  31, f1 at  20
  499 ms  leader at  50, f1 at  20   (the link comes back at 500 ms)

  526 ms  leader at  53, f1 at  53   (entries 21 to 53 arrived at 525)

Again, but the leader keeps only its last 20 log entries when f1 comes back:
  f1 asks for entries after 20: leader: entries after 20 are gone (oldest kept: 81); rebuild from a snapshot
  f1 restored from a snapshot at position 100; rows match the leader: true

The gap is the signal. Entry 52 arrives while f1 is at 20, so f1 refuses to apply it and asks for everything after 20. One round trip later, it has caught up. When the leader has thrown those entries away, the position alone is no use, and f1 must start again from a snapshot. With 90 entries kept, entries 21 to 100 are all still there, and f1 applies 80 entries instead.

sections.h: When the leader dies: notice, choose, redirect, and what each step breaks
sections.html:
Sooner or later the leader dies. The followers can still answer questions, but nothing records a payment until one becomes the leader. That's failover, in three steps: notice, choose and redirect. The stepper below shows all three.

Notice. Nothing tells a follower that the leader is dead. It only notices that the leader has gone quiet: no new entries, and no heartbeat, the small "I'm still here" message a leader sends every few seconds. So every system waits for a timeout. By default, MongoDB's followers hold an election, a vote on who takes over, after 10 seconds of silence. Its manual says choosing a new leader should not typically take more than 12 seconds. Patroni, a program often used to run failover for PostgreSQL, gives the leader a 30-second lease: a promise that runs out unless the leader renews it.

Too long a timeout, and payments fail for all of it. Too short, and a leader that's only slow gets replaced, and its load lands on a follower that may be struggling too. (A Java program can pause for a second to clear out unused memory.) So many teams fail over by hand. Detecting failure, in the Faults, time and truth track, shows why no timeout fits every case.

Choose. The follower with the highest position loses the least. With semi-synchronous replication, the follower the leader waited for has every acknowledged payment. Agreeing on that choice while some machines can't reach others is a hard problem called consensus.

Redirect. Card readers must now reach the new leader. A name can be moved to point at it (DNS, the internet's phone book, from the Computer networking track). Or a proxy, a program in the middle, forwards each request to whichever machine leads. Or a library in the client asks each machine. The old leader, when it comes back, must rejoin as a follower.

Each step can hurt. Under asynchronous replication, the new leader lacks the old leader's last entries. When the old leader returns, its extra entries clash with the new history, and the usual fix throws them away. MongoDB writes them to a rollback folder for a person to read; PostgreSQL's pg_rewind tool discards them. Card readers were told OK for payments that no longer exist.

Payment numbers get reused, too. Each new record gets the next number from a counter, which databases call an auto-increment id. The new leader's counter starts after the highest id it holds, so it hands out the lost payments' ids again. If another system keeps those ids, such as a cache (a saved copy of answers, kept for speed), they now point at different records. GitHub hit this in September 2012. An out-of-date MySQL server was promoted, and its ids no longer matched what a Redis cache held. For seven minutes, 16 private code projects were visible to people outside their teams.

And there can be two leaders. If the old one was only cut off, not dead, it may still take payments from card readers that can reach it. Two machines now accept writes and hand out the same ids. That's split brain. The fix is called fencing: make sure the old leader can't write, by powering it off, cutting it off or letting its lease run out, before the new one starts. Lesson 4 shows split brain on two real PostgreSQL servers, and the Faults track's lesson Leases, locks and fencing tokens shows how to fence properly.

Two leaders write two histories. Fence the old one first, then promote.

GitHub's outage of 21 October 2018 had all of this at once. At 22:52 UTC, maintenance on network equipment cut the link between its East Coast hub and its main East Coast data center (a building full of servers) for 43 seconds. Its failover tool, Orchestrator, which decides by majority vote, promoted new leaders on the West Coast. Programs wrote to them for nearly 40 minutes, while the old East Coast leaders held several seconds of writes the West never got.

Now each side had writes the other lacked, and East Coast programs were too slow with every database call crossing the country. GitHub chose its data over its uptime. The site was slow or partly broken for 24 hours and 11 minutes while the team restored and merged the two histories. One of its busiest groups of servers had 954 writes in the affected window. Afterwards, GitHub stopped Orchestrator from promoting leaders across regions.

That's the limit of today's tools: copies that don't wait can lose payments at failover, and copies that wait make every payment slower. The Consistency and consensus track closes the gap by waiting for a majority. First, we'll open the log and ask what one entry should say.

Replication is asynchronous, so each follower has what the network has brought it so far: f1, 20 ms away, has applied up to position 246, and f2, 50 ms away, up to 238. These are the lab's numbers: a payment every 4 ms and a crash at 1,001 ms.

frames.say: The leader's machine dies. Entries 247 to 250 were still on their way to f1, and they die with it. Their card readers already heard OK. From the followers' side, nothing looks wrong yet. They hear nothing at all.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">1,001 ms + timeout</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">leader: crashed</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">250 on its disk</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">unreachable</text><rect class="box-a" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 246</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">no heartbeat: dead?</text><rect class="box-a" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 238</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">no heartbeat: dead?</text><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="120" x2="408" y2="78" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="150" x2="408" y2="192" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">every write fails until a follower takes over</text></svg>
frames.say: Notice. The followers can't tell a dead leader from a slow one or a broken link. So they wait for a timeout: 10 seconds by default in MongoDB, a 30-second lease with Patroni for PostgreSQL. Every payment fails for that long.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">choose</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">leader: crashed</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">250 on its disk</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">unreachable</text><rect class="box-a" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: new leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 246</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">next id: 247</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 238</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="120" x2="408" y2="78" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="150" x2="408" y2="192" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">f2 catches up from f1: entries 239 to 246</text></svg>
frames.say: Choose. The follower with the highest position loses the least, so f1 becomes the leader. f2 starts following f1 and fetches entries 239 to 246 from it. f1's id counter starts again after the highest id it holds: 247.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">redirect</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">leader: crashed</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">250 on its disk</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">unreachable</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">refund-1 got id 247</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">the cache still says id 247 is pay-247; the database says refund-1</text></svg>
frames.say: Redirect. Card readers find f1 (through a moved name, a proxy, or a library that asks each machine) and carry on. The next four records, refunds, get ids 247 to 250: the ids of the lost payments. A cache filled before the crash still says those ids belong to the old payments. This is GitHub's 2012 failure, in miniature.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">later</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">old leader: back</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">thinks it leads</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">different 247 to 250</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">two leaders accept writes: split brain</text></svg>
frames.say: The old leader's machine restarts, or its network heals. It still has its own entries 247 to 250, and nothing has told it that it was replaced. Card readers that still have its address can send payments to it. Two machines accept writes and hand out the same ids: split brain.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">fence and rejoin</text><rect class="box-dim" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">old leader: fenced</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">rewound to 246</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">now follows f1</text><rect class="box-ok" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">the only writer</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-ok" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">one leader again; 4 acknowledged payments are gone for good</text></svg>
frames.say: The fix is to fence the old leader before it can take writes (power it off, cut it off, or let its lease run out) and bring it back only as a follower. First it must throw away its own 247 to 250, as PostgreSQL's pg_rewind does. Those four payments were acknowledged and are gone for good: that's the price of asynchronous replication, paid at failover.

try.title: Lose four payments, then reuse their ids
steps: From the labs folder, run the first command below. It's the stepper's three machines: after the crash, it promotes the best follower and writes four refunds. A cache stands in for GitHub's Redis. Each time a card reader heard OK, the cache saved id -> payment.
Predict the ids the four refunds get. Then run the second command, where the leader waits for one follower, and compare.

code.title: in the labs folder
code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l01.demo.FailoverDemoKt -q ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l01.demo.FailoverDemoKt -Pargs='sync' -q

try.expect:
mode: asynchronous
1,001 ms  the leader dies at position 250; clients have heard OK for 250 payments
          f1 has applied up to position 246
          f2 has applied up to position 238
          promote f1, the most up to date; its next id is 247
          acknowledged but not on f1: [pay-247, pay-248, pay-249, pay-250]

 1101 ms  the new leader stores refund-1 as id 247  <- the cache says id 247 is pay-247
 1102 ms  the new leader stores refund-2 as id 248  <- the cache says id 248 is pay-248
 1103 ms  the new leader stores refund-3 as id 249  <- the cache says id 249 is pay-249
 1104 ms  the new leader stores refund-4 as id 250  <- the cache says id 250 is pay-250

Four acknowledged payments are gone, and their ids now mean one thing in the database and another in the cache. With sync, card readers heard OK for 241 payments, and nothing acknowledged is lost. None of the reused ids (247 to 250) is in the cache, because no card reader was ever told that those payments existed.

opening:
Picture a café. You tap your card for a coffee, and a small company's program records the payment: which card, which shop, how much and when. It keeps them in a database, a program that stores records and answers questions about them, on one computer.

One morning, that computer's disk fails. Every payment since last night's backup is gone, and no card works anywhere until someone sets up a new machine.

The fix sounds easy: keep a copy on a second computer. Copying a file is easy, so it feels solved. But payments keep arriving, hundreds a second, and the copies must change in step: in the same order, with no gaps, and without anyone waiting too long.

In Durable execution, we wrote down every step of an order so a crash couldn't erase it. That record still lived on one machine. In this lesson, we'll keep copies on three machines, let one decide the order, choose when to say OK, and then crash the one in charge. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a payments database on one machine and a disk that died. Copies fix that, as long as one leader decides the order. But every copy is a little behind, and the moment the leader says OK decides what its death can take with it.

Next time an app tells you "saved", ask: saved on how many machines? If you have this course's PostgreSQL pair running (the next lesson starts it), run SELECT application_name, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication; on the leader. It lists each follower, and says whether the leader waits for it.

Next, we'll open one entry of the log, and ask what it should say so that every follower ends up with exactly the leader's data.

compare.title: Waiting for one follower: MySQL and PostgreSQL

a.label: MySQL 8.4
a.title: my.cnf on the source (plugin installed)
a.html: rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_for_replica_count = 1 # default rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point = AFTER_SYNC # default: after the binlog # sync, before the engine commit rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 10000 # ms, default # the replica acks once the events are flushed to its relay log # timeout without an ack: the source reverts to asynchronous # SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_status'; 1 = waiting, 0 = async

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: postgresql.conf on the primary
b.html: synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)' synchronous_commit = on # default: wait until a standby has # flushed the commit's WAL to disk # (remote_write, remote_apply: other points) # no timeout: with no listed standby connected, # every COMMIT waits until one comes back # SELECT application_name, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication;

compare.note: PostgreSQL calls a follower a standby, and MySQL calls its leader the source. Both settings make the leader wait until one follower has the change on its disk, so on a good day they promise the same thing. They differ when no follower answers. MySQL gives up after 10 seconds and stops waiting, which keeps payments flowing and quietly drops the promise. PostgreSQL keeps every change waiting, which keeps the promise and stops the payments. Neither is wrong, and each needs two things. A second follower, so that one slow machine doesn't trip the timeout. And an alert on the status query at the bottom of each box, so that a person hears about it when the leader stops waiting. Choose MySQL's timeout on purpose, too: a short one keeps payments fast and accepts some loss, and a very long one keeps the promise and stops payments.

worked.title: How much would a failover lose right now?

steps.say: First find the gap between the leader and its best follower, as a log position and as time. On PostgreSQL, the leader reports both for every follower. pg_wal_lsn_diff subtracts two positions and gives the gap in bytes.
steps.code: -- on the primary: bytes and time each standby is behind SELECT application_name, sync_state, pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), flush_lsn) AS flush_behind_bytes, flush_lag, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;

steps.say: On MySQL, check that semi-synchronous replication is really on, not only switched on in the settings, and count the commits that went through without any follower's confirmation.
steps.code: SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_status'; -- 1: waiting for replicas, 0: fell back to async SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_tx'; -- commits that were never acknowledged by a replica

steps.say: On MongoDB, the shell (the command line you type queries into) prints how far each follower is behind the leader.
steps.code: rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo() // each secondary's last applied oplog time and lag behind the primary

steps.say: Turn the gap into payments. Say the follower's flush lag, the time between the leader writing an entry and the follower having it on disk, is typically 250 ms, and the company records 400 payments a second. Then an asynchronous failover at a typical moment loses about 100 acknowledged payments. At a bad moment, with 30 seconds of lag during a catch-up, it loses about 12,000. (These numbers are made up for the example.)
steps.code:
lost ~= write rate x lag of the follower you would promote
       = 400 payments/s x 0.25 s = 100 payments   (typical)
       = 400 payments/s x 30 s  = 12,000 payments (during a catch-up)

steps.say: Decide for each kind of change. A card payment can wait for a follower. A note of which page a shop owner opened can stay asynchronous, because losing a few costs nothing. PostgreSQL lets each transaction (a group of changes that become final together) choose for itself with SET LOCAL.
steps.code: -- PostgreSQL: choose per transaction BEGIN; SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = on; -- authorization: wait for a standby INSERT INTO payments (card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (7, 3, 1250, 'succeeded', now()); COMMIT;

lab.title: A leader, two followers and a failover, on pretend time
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. They need no Docker and finish in about a second, because Sim runs pretend time and never sleeps. All 22 fail. Read Replication.kt first. Cluster already sends entries over links with a delay, keeps the messages on each link in order, drops messages to and from crashed machines, and answers catch-up requests.

Exercise 1, Node.apply: apply entries in position order, skip the ones the node already has, and stop at a gap. CatchUpTest builds a follower from a snapshot plus entriesAfter(position), and cuts a follower off for 300 ms.

Exercise 2, Cluster.isAcknowledged: when may the leader say OK? Asynchronous: at once. Synchronous: once enough followers have confirmed. Semi-synchronous: after one confirmation or the timeout, whichever comes first, and after a timeout it switches itself off. AckTest checks the waits in this lesson's table.

Exercise 3, Cluster.failover: promote the live follower with the highest position, reset its id counter, and list the acknowledged writes it never had. FailoverTest counts them for each choice and reproduces the reused ids. Then the two tests in FailoverPropertyTest each try 200 random delays and crash times.
hints: apply: loop over the entries. continue when entry.position <= position, break when entry.position != position + 1, and otherwise put the row, add the entry to log, move position and count it.

isAcknowledged: write a local fun has(f: Node) = (confirmed[f.name] ?: 0) >= entry.position, then a when (mode). For semi-sync, the order of the checks matters: switched off, then any follower has it, then the timeout (which sets semiSyncOn = false and returns true).

failover: followers.filter { it.alive }.maxByOrNull { it.position } keeps the first of two equals. Set nextId from rows.keys.maxOrNull(), work out acknowledged.filter { it.entry.position > chosen.position } before you call promote, and return both.

If a property test fails, jqwik (the library that runs those random tests) prints the smallest delays and crash time that break it. Copy that case into a plain test, and print cluster.acknowledged and each follower's position.

drill.title: The OK rule, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write isAcknowledged(entry, waitedMs) for the three choices: asynchronous, synchronous to N followers, and MySQL-style semi-synchronous, with a timeout that switches the leader to asynchronous. confirmed[name] is the highest position each follower has confirmed.

answer.html: fun isAcknowledged(entry: LogEntry, waitedMs: Long): Boolean { fun has(f: Node) = (confirmed[f.name] ?: 0) >= entry.position return when (mode) { Mode.Async -> true // the leader's disk is enough is Mode.Sync -> followers.count(::has) >= mode.followers is Mode.SemiSync -> when { !semiSyncOn -> true // already fallen back followers.any(::has) -> true waitedMs >= mode.timeoutMs -> { semiSyncOn = false; true } // silent fallback else -> false } } }

recap: A replica is a copy of the whole database that keeps up with every change. Copies survive a dead machine, answer questions near the people asking and share the load. All the difficulty is in the changes.
Single-leader replication: one leader puts every change in a numbered log, and each follower applies the log in order. A follower's position says how up to date it is.

Asynchronous replication says OK before any follower has the change, so a failover can lose acknowledged payments. Waiting for every follower lets one slow machine stop all payments. Semi-synchronous waits for one, and MySQL's quietly stops waiting after a 10-second timeout.

A new follower is a snapshot plus every log entry after the snapshot's exact position. A follower that comes back catches up from its position if the leader still has those entries, and otherwise needs a new snapshot.

Failover is notice (a timeout), choose (the highest position) and redirect. It can lose acknowledged writes, reuse ids that other systems still hold, and create split brain unless the old leader is fenced.
The limit: with copies that lag, a failover still trades lost payments against waiting. GitHub's 43-second network cut in 2018 became 24 hours and 11 minutes of trouble.

explain.prompt: A friend who runs a shop asks why "the payments company keeps three copies of the database" doesn't mean a payment can never be lost, or that payments never stop. Explain it in plain words.
explain.answer: Only one of the three copies, the leader, takes new payments. It puts them in order, and the other two copy that order. Usually the leader tells the card reader OK as soon as it has saved the payment itself, and the copies get it a few milliseconds later. If the leader's machine dies inside those milliseconds, the payment is on no machine that's still running, although the customer was told it went through. The leader can wait until one copy confirms. That costs a little time on every payment and closes the gap, but then a stuck copy slows or stops payments, and some databases quietly stop waiting after a timeout. When the leader dies, nothing takes payments until a copy is promoted, and that only happens after a timeout, so there are seconds of failed payments. Promotion has traps too: a copy that's behind can hand out payment numbers again, and if the old leader comes back and keeps taking payments, there are two different histories. So three copies make losing everything very unlikely. Losing the last few payments, and a short stop, are still possible unless the company pays for copies that wait and for a careful failover.

deeper.html:
Most databases follow this lesson's design under their own names. MySQL is another popular free database, MongoDB stores each record as a document of named values, Redis keeps its data in memory, and Kafka keeps logs of messages for other programs to read. An offset is a count from the start of the log:

Program The leader The followers The log A position looks like
PostgreSQL primary standbys write-ahead log (WAL) a byte count, 0/50DF770
MySQL source replicas binary log a file and an offset, or a transaction id
MongoDB primary secondaries oplog a timestamp
Redis master replicas replication stream a byte offset
Kafka partition leader followers the partition an offset

Redis's version is in the Caching track's lesson Persistence and replication. Oracle's database, which big companies buy, does the same with a feature called Data Guard.

Kafka has its own version of this lesson's choice. With acks=all, a write waits for every follower in the in-sync replica set, the followers that are keeping up. That set can shrink to the leader alone, and then acks=all waits for nobody. A setting, min.insync.replicas, refuses writes when the set gets too small. The Messaging track's lesson The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR covers both.

Redis's cluster mode picks a new leader with a rule you can read in one line. Each follower waits 500 ms, plus up to 500 ms at random, plus one second for each follower that's more up to date than it (its rank). So the most up-to-date follower, rank 0, usually asks the other leaders for votes first, and it needs a majority of them.

Databases built on object storage change the picture. A growing set of systems (WarpStream and Bufstream for Kafka-style logs, SlateDB, Turbopuffer) keep their log and data in S3-style object storage, a cloud service that stores files and keeps its own copies of them. They use a conditional write, which succeeds only if the file is still the version you last saw, to decide which machine is the leader. Nothing is copied between the machines' own disks at all: the object store's copies give the durability, and the conditional write is the fencing. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6 has a sidebar on this design.

Raft-based databases (CockroachDB, TiDB, etcd, YugabyteDB) are single-leader too, for each range of keys, but they wait for a majority on every write and elect leaders by majority vote. That closes both of this lesson's failover holes at once. An acknowledged write is on a majority, and any new leader must win a majority, which must include a machine that has the write. The Consistency and consensus track builds this from the ground up.

The words "synchronous" and "semi-synchronous" mean different things in different manuals. MySQL's semi-synchronous replication waits for a follower to receive the entry and flush it to disk. PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit = remote_write waits for less, and remote_apply for more. Before you trust a setting, find out exactly which of the points in this lesson's figure it waits for, and what it does when no follower answers.

If you run MongoDB: writes with w: 1 are acknowledged by the leader alone. When a leader is replaced before it has copied them, they're rolled back and written to a rollback folder on disk for someone to inspect. The default since MongoDB 5.0 is w: "majority", which makes that much rarer.
